query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unique combination of high plasticity and machinability with relatively low hardness and strength in equimolar (or nearly equimolar) CoCrFeNiTi is governed by the absence of nano-scale precipitates or ordering within its single-phase solid solution. In other words, without secondary phases to impede dislocation motion, the alloy deforms primarily via unhindered dislocation glide, resulting in lower strength and hardness despite favorable ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produced in a homogeneous, disordered single-phase solid solution state with minimal secondary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled heat treatment (aging) designed to induce nano-scale precipitate formation or local ordering.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in the temperature range of 25 °C to 600 °C under compressive and tensile loading; comparison of as-cast (untreated) samples to heat-treated (aged) samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or lack thereof) of nano-scale precipitates or ordered regions within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: In the untreated alloy, the absence of precipitates permits easy dislocation motion, leading to high ductility but reduced strengthening. Inducing nano-scale precipitates via aging should allow these particles to act as barriers to dislocation motion (Orowan strengthening), thereby increasing hardness and compressive strength while reducing plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated alloy will develop discernible nano-scale precipitates and exhibit a measurable increase in hardness and compressive strength relative to the as-cast alloy, accompanied by a reduction in ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase CoCrFeNiTi alloy at room temperature with its known combination of favorable plasticity/machinability but lower hardness and strength.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloys in their simple solid-solution state; in alloys where multiple phases or significant compositional deviations are present, different strengthening mechanisms could dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact heat treatment parameters (temperature, time) needed to reproducibly induce the optimal amount of nano-precipitation without degrading overall ductility are not yet determined, and the quantitative changes in mechanical properties need further exploration.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples: one set as-cast (control) and a second set that undergoes a specifically designed aging heat treatment aimed at inducing nano-scale precipitate formation. Characterize the microstructure and mechanical properties of both sets.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect the presence and distribution of nano-scale precipitates or ordering.
Microhardness testing to determine hardness differences between samples.
Compressive and tensile mechanical tests in the 25 °C to 600 °C range to evaluate differences in strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show significant nano-scale precipitate formation or if they do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in hardness and compressive strength (with a corresponding decrease in ductility) compared to the as-cast samples, then the hypothesis that the absence of precipitates is responsible for the mechanical behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures.

High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. At 300 K and 600 K, the ordered lattice structure of the high entropy alloy coating material is basically the same, and thus its hardness is basically the same. Abstract High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit excellent properties such as high strength, good ductility, superior corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, making them highly promising for applications in the aerospace, energy, and automotive industries. Among them, the FeNiCrMn HEA demonstrates outstanding corrosion resistance while eliminating the expensive Co element present in the “Cantor” alloy, significantly reducing costs. However, current research on the FeNiCrMn HEA has primarily focused on its corrosion resistance, with relatively limited studies on its mechanical properties. This paper investigated the effects of different crystal orientations, temperatures, and strain rates on the mechanical properties and plastic deformation mechanisms of an equiatomic FeNiCrMn HEA using molecular dynamics simulations. The results revealed that the FeNiCrMn HEA exhibited significant anisotropy under loading along different orientations, with the maximum yield stress observed along the <11-1> direction. Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
